buy2-two-sets-of-weights-in-one-bag.reason: Opens on Deuteronomy 25 and why possession is banned; the plain test (one standard applied in both directions, side by side on paper) only arrives near the end.
buy2-two-sets-of-weights-in-one-bag.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is your property math honest in both directions? Only if you would value the same building the same way whether you are buying it or selling it. When your numbers move depending on which side of the table you sit on, the math is not honest, even if every single number can be defended. Here is why the Word says so, and how to check yourself.
buy2-two-sets-of-weights-in-one-bag.example: ONE BUILDING, TWO DIRECTIONS. A small rental clears $60,000 a year after its expenses. The cap rate is the yearly return you expect on the price you pay. Buying it, you insist on 9 percent: $60,000 divided by 0.09 is about $666,700. Selling the same kind of building, you quote 7.5 percent: $60,000 divided by 0.075 is $800,000. Same income, same kind of building, $133,300 apart. That gap is the second stone, and now it has a price.
buy2-two-sets-of-weights-in-one-bag.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is your property math honest in both directions? It is when one valuation sheet does both jobs: the same cap rate, the same vacancy, the same repairs and the same costs, whether the building is coming to you or leaving you. Before you change an assumption, ask whether you would accept it from across the table. Then every number you use is one you could show the other side, and the honest weight carries its promise: length of days in the land.

teen.open: The title asks a fair question. Is your math about a house the same when you buy it and when you sell it? It should be.
teen.close: So use one set of numbers whether you are buying or selling. If your math changes with your side of the deal, that is the second weight Yahweh forbids.

senior.open: The title asks whether your property math is honest both ways. It is honest only when the standard you buy by is the same one you sell by.
senior.close: So the question in the title has a plain answer. Your property math is honest in both directions when the standard you buy by is the standard you sell by, line for line.

buy1-abraham-refused-the-gift-and-paid-i.reason: Opens on the Genesis 23 narrative and the elements of the close; the why (a gift leaves mismatched memories; price paid in public becomes title) arrives only in the second half.
buy1-abraham-refused-the-gift-and-paid-i.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why would Abraham refuse a free field? Because a gift with no price leaves two different memories behind it. The giver keeps a claim that was never written down, and the receiver carries a debt he can never pay off. By naming a price, paying it in public, and having it recorded, Abraham turned goodwill into title: ownership no one could dispute later. Here is how Genesis 23 shows it.
buy1-abraham-refused-the-gift-and-paid-i.example: ONE FAVOR, TWO MEMORIES. Say a relative hands you a strip of land beside your house for nothing, on a handshake. Years later an heir, or a bank, asks how you came to own it. The relative remembers a loan; you remember a gift; nothing is written. Now say instead you paid a named price, described the strip exactly, had it witnessed and recorded. The same question gets a one-line answer, and the friendship never has to carry it.
buy1-abraham-refused-the-gift-and-paid-i.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why would Abraham refuse a free field? Because he wanted the field to be his beyond argument, and a gift could never do that. He named the price, weighed the silver in the money the market used, described the land to its borders, had it witnessed, and made it sure at the city gate (Genesis 23:16-18). That is the case for paying in public: it protects the title and the friendship both. Deal the same way, and your ownership will never depend on goodwill surviving a dispute.

teen.open: Why would anyone turn down free land? Abraham did, because a gift with no price can turn into an argument later. Paying in public made the field clearly his.
teen.close: So the answer is simple. Abraham paid a fair price, in public, with witnesses, so nobody could ever argue about who owned the field. Clear deals keep friendships safe.

senior.open: Why would Abraham turn down a field freely offered? Because an unpriced gift leaves an unwritten claim on one side and an unpayable obligation on the other. A price paid in public settles both.
senior.close: So the title’s question has its answer. Abraham refused the gift because he wanted a title, not a favor: priced, weighed, described, witnessed and recorded. A deal made that way outlasts every memory of it.

buy3-it-is-naught-it-is-naught-saith-the.reason: Says early that the boast is the evidence, but the line between honest defect and false verdict comes mid-lesson and the before-you-speak test only near the end; ends on reputation, not the test.
buy3-it-is-naught-it-is-naught-saith-the.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How does the buyer’s discount lie get caught? By his own mouth. He calls the property worthless while buying, then boasts once he has gone (Proverbs 20:14), and the two statements convict each other. Stating a real defect is honest negotiation; speaking a verdict on value you do not hold is the lie. The test before you speak: would you be content to hear it repeated back to you in a month?
buy3-it-is-naught-it-is-naught-saith-the.example: TWO SENTENCES ABOUT ONE ROOF. One buyer says: the roof has three years left, here is the estimate, and the price should reflect it. That is a fact about the property, and it passes the test. Another buyer says: nobody wants a building like this, while wanting it himself. That is a verdict on value he does not hold. A month later, when the seller hears what was paid and how it was bragged about, the first buyer is still trusted and the second is not.
buy3-it-is-naught-it-is-naught-saith-the.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What catches the discount lie? The buyer’s own boast, because the proverb simply sets his two statements side by side. You remain free to negotiate, to keep your ceiling to yourself, and to press hard on every real defect. What you may not do is speak a verdict on value you do not hold. So before you say it, ask whether you would be content for the seller to hear it repeated back to you in a month. If yes, say it. If not, keep your reputation; it is the cheapest advantage you have.

teen.open: The buyer says it is worthless, then brags later about his great deal. The brag gives him away. He never thought it was worthless.
teen.close: So the lie gets caught by the buyer’s own words. Before you say something to get a lower price, ask yourself: would I be okay if the seller heard this again next month?

senior.open: How is the buyer’s discount lie exposed? By his own boast. He calls the property worthless while buying it, then praises his bargain afterward, and the two statements convict each other.
senior.close: So the title’s question is answered. Name real defects freely, but never speak a verdict on value you do not hold. The test is simple: would you be content to hear your words repeated back to you in a month?

buy5-haste-is-the-most-expensive-thing-i.reason: Builds the two proverbs first; what they reveal about closing early (haste = closing before the truth arrives; unweighed risk lands on others) and the written discipline come late and in pieces.
buy5-haste-is-the-most-expensive-thing-i.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What do Proverbs 21:5 and 28:20 reveal about closing before you know the truth? That haste leads to want, and that haste to be rich costs a man his innocence. In a deal, haste means closing before the facts that would change the price have arrived. A risk you never weigh does not disappear; your family, lender, tenants or partner end up paying it. Here is how the Word shows it, and the simple discipline that answers it.
buy5-haste-is-the-most-expensive-thing-i.example: ONE LIST, TWO DATES. Say closing is set for the 30th. Your list reads: inspection report, back the 22nd; rent roll checked against actual deposits, the 25th; title work, the 3rd of next month. Title lands after closing. The broker says another offer is coming. That tells you about the seller, not the building. Either move the closing past the 3rd, or admit on your own paper that you are wagering on the title.
buy5-haste-is-the-most-expensive-thing-i.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. When a deal rushes you, Proverbs points to what the hasty man never does: consider the downside (Proverbs 28:22). Urgency tells you about the seller’s situation, not about the building. So write down every item still unverified, the inspection, the rent roll, title, the estimates, the estoppels, with a date beside each, and set that list against the closing date. If the closing comes first, you are wagering, not buying. Slow enough to find out is the diligent man’s speed, and his thoughts tend to plenty (Proverbs 21:5).

teen.open: When a deal pushes you to hurry, Proverbs says slow down. Rushing means signing before you know the facts, and someone always pays for what you skipped.
teen.close: So here is the answer. Write down what you still have not checked, and when you will know it. If you have to sign before then, you are gambling, not buying.

senior.open: What do these proverbs reveal about a rushed closing? That haste leads to want, and that refusing to weigh your own risk quietly hands it to others, which is why the hasty man shall not be innocent.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Close only after the truth has arrived. List what remains unverified with a date beside each item, set it against the closing date, and let urgency tell you about the seller, never about the building.

buy6-what-borrowing-makes-you-and-what-i.reason: Spends the first half on Deuteronomy 15:6 and Romans 13:8; the reserves question in the title appears only past the midpoint, and the lesson ends on the pastoral plan and the previous lesson.
buy6-what-borrowing-makes-you-and-what-i.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How many months could your reserves really hold? Only you can write that number, and you should: count how many months of full vacancy, or how large a repair failure, your cash would survive. The Word treats borrowing as a position, not just a payment; the lender holds part of your decisions (Deuteronomy 15:6). That one number shows how much of the decision is still yours. Here is how the Word sets it out.
buy6-what-borrowing-makes-you-and-what-i.example: ONE LINE ON ONE PAGE. Say a rental’s loan, taxes, insurance and upkeep run $3,000 a month, and you hold $9,000 in reserve. With every unit empty, the reserve covers three months. That is your number. If one failed roof would cost more than $9,000, your position is weaker than the monthly payment ever showed. Written down, the number tells you how long the decisions stay yours before the lender’s calendar becomes yours.
buy6-what-borrowing-makes-you-and-what-i.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. How many months could your reserves really hold? Write it down: the months of full vacancy, or the size of a capital failure, your cash would survive. The Word permits borrowing and does not call it sin, but it names it as the ruled position (Deuteronomy 15:6) and points toward owing no one anything but love (Romans 13:8). That number is the distance between holding a tool and being held by one. Grow it before the next purchase, and the decisions stay in your hands.

teen.open: Borrowing is more than a monthly payment. It gives the lender a say in your choices. So ask: if no rent came in at all, how many months could you last?
teen.close: That number is the answer to the title. The more months your savings can cover, the more your choices stay yours. Borrowing is not a sin, but keep growing that number.

senior.open: How many months could your reserves carry you if every unit sat empty? The Word frames borrowing as a position, the ruled side of Deuteronomy 15:6, and that number measures how much of the position is still yours.
senior.close: So the title’s question deserves a written answer. Know how many months of full vacancy, or how large a capital failure, your reserves would survive. Borrowing is permitted, not sin; but a reserve that grows before the next purchase keeps the decisions in your own hands.

buy7-give-a-portion-to-seven-and-also-to.reason: The survival test that answers the title (if you can name the one event, the allocation has failed) arrives mid-lesson after the yield and tension discussion; ends on reserves without restating the answer.
buy7-give-a-portion-to-seven-and-also-to.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Could one event wipe out everything you own? Here is the test: if you can name that event in one sentence, a fire, a plant closing, one note called, then yes, and your allocation has already failed Ecclesiastes 11:2. Solomon says spread your portions, to seven and also to eight, because you do not know what trouble is coming. This applies before you are rich, and it starts with cash set aside.
buy7-give-a-portion-to-seven-and-also-to.example: THE ONE-SENTENCE TEST. Say you own two rentals on the same street, both loans with the same lender, six tenants, four of them working at one plant, and no cash set aside. Ask the question and the answer comes at once: the plant closes. That sentence is the warning. A third building on the same street does not fix it. Three months of expenses sitting in the bank begins to.
buy7-give-a-portion-to-seven-and-also-to.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Could one event wipe out everything you own? Not if your portions are spread so that no single fire, closing, lender call or judgement can end the whole estate. A large position is allowed; a position one event can finish is not. Separate properties and streets, tenants with different employers, staggered loan dates, insurance actually read, and cash in the bank. And start before you are rich: three months of expenses, sitting still, is the eighth portion that keeps the other seven standing.

teen.open: Could one bad event take everything you have? If you can name that event right now, the answer is yes. Solomon says spread things out, because nobody knows what is coming.
teen.close: So the answer is no, if you spread things out. And it starts now, before you have much: put some money aside and leave it there for the hard day.

senior.open: Could a single event end your whole estate? If you can name it in a sentence, it could. Ecclesiastes 11:2 tells us to spread our portions, seven and then eight, because we do not know what evil is coming.
senior.close: So the title’s question has its answer. Arrange what you hold so no one event can take it all, and begin before you feel rich, with three months of expenses held still in reserve.

buy8-he-that-sweareth-to-his-own-hurt-an.reason: Explains Psalm 15:4 early but the practical answer (perform or settle openly, never silence; earlier disciplines keep promises keepable) comes late; ends on why the lesson is last in the course.
buy8-he-that-sweareth-to-his-own-hurt-an.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Will your word still hold when the deal turns against you? Psalm 15:4 commends the man who swears to his own hurt and changes not, and Numbers 30:2 says do all that came out of your mouth. So it must hold. If you truly cannot perform, there is one other honorable road: go back to the other party, say so plainly, and settle it openly. What is ruled out is silence.
buy8-he-that-sweareth-to-his-own-hurt-an.example: THE REPAIR THAT SLIDES. Say you promised at signing to make a repair, and then a cost overrun eats your margin. Week one, it moves down the list. Week two, a call goes unreturned. Nobody said no, but the promise is decaying. Psalm 15 leaves two roads: do the repair at your own cost, or call the other party, say plainly you cannot this month, and agree the settlement together. Silence is the one road closed.
buy8-he-that-sweareth-to-his-own-hurt-an.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Will your word hold when it costs you? It will if you refuse both the flat no and the slow drift: the change order, the slipping repair, the date that moves, the call not returned. Perform, or speak plainly and settle openly. And it holds most surely when you made it keepable from the start: an honest price, one standard both ways, truthful talk, no surety, facts verified before closing. Integrity at the hard moment is mostly the fruit of decisions made when nothing was at stake.

teen.open: What if keeping your promise starts to cost you? Psalm 15 praises the person who keeps it anyway, even when it hurts.
teen.close: So yes, your word should hold. If you truly cannot do it, go and say so honestly and work it out together. Never just go quiet and let it slide.

senior.open: Will your word hold when the deal turns against you? Psalm 15:4 commends the one who swears to his own hurt and changes not, so the standard is to perform even when it costs.
senior.close: So the title’s question is answered. Keep your word, or go to the other party, say plainly you cannot, and settle openly. Silence and slow drift are the roads closed, and honest decisions made earlier keep the hard promise keepable.

buy4-surety-the-trap-you-talk-yourself-i.reason: Answers at once (the trap closes at agreement; snared by the words of your mouth) but ends on the generous alternative to co-signing rather than landing the locked-in answer.
buy4-surety-the-trap-you-talk-yourself-i.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Did your yes already lock you in? Yes. Proverbs 6:1-2 puts the snare at the words of your mouth, not at the missed payment. The moment you sign the guarantee, co-sign the mortgage, or promise a lender you will cover a shortfall, the exposure exists and someone else holds the timing. So if you are already surety, work to be released now, while nothing has failed. And when love wants to help, give what you can afford to lose, in an amount and at a time you choose.

teen.open: Does signing for someone else’s loan trap you, even if they never miss a payment? Proverbs 6 says yes. The trap closes the moment you say yes.
teen.close: So your yes is what locks you in. If you want to help someone, give what you can afford to give, instead of promising money you cannot control.

senior.open: Does a guarantee bind you before anything goes wrong? Proverbs 6:1-2 says you are snared by the words of your mouth, at the moment of agreement, long before any payment is missed.
senior.close: So the answer is yes. The signature is the snare. If you stand surety now, seek release without delay; and when love wants to help, give a sum you choose, at a time you choose, rather than pledge your whole future.
